title: Cybersecurity Daily Briefing
description: Actively exploited vulnerabilities, major incidents, and threat trends relevant to enterprise and federal networks.
readFirst: Covers Oct. 26–Nov. 2. New: CISA on Oct. 30 added two Ivanti Connect Secure bugs, one due Nov. 2 and one due Nov. 13, and Cisco Talos on Oct. 31 described the VOLTA stealer, which asks Claude to rank stolen data. Federal News Network reported Oct. 30 that a CISA official called Chainguard's early PHP patch release dangerous. The GitLab and Cisco firewall KEV items were removed because their Nov. 1 due dates have passed, and the Oct. 28 Linux kernel bug was removed because its Oct. 31 due date has passed. The VMware ESX logging bug from that alert remains due Nov. 11 and is on the partners page. The Oct. 26 CISA 2030 strategy item was dropped so the trends subsection stayed within four items. No new public update on the DMDC personnel breach was found.

items.headline: CISA adds two Ivanti Connect Secure bugs, one due Nov. 2 and one due Nov. 13
items.summary: CISA said Oct. 30 it added CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527, both in Ivanti Connect Secure, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The catalog sets a due date of Nov. 2 for CVE-2026-111357, requires forensic triage, and says a local authenticated attacker could escalate privileges. It sets a due date of Nov. 13 for CVE-2026-118527, does not require forensic triage, and says a remote authenticated attacker can upload files to a known location. SecurityWeek reported Nov. 2 that Ivanti rates the bugs 8.8 and 4.3, that fixes are in Connect Secure 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6, and that Ivanti said the latest release addresses the vulnerabilities that were chained and exploited in the wild with CVE-2026-104935.

items.headline: Cisco Talos: the VOLTA stealer asks Claude to rank what a victim is worth
items.summary: Cisco Talos said Oct. 31 that a self-deleting Windows infostealer it calls VOLTA-AUTODOXER sends a structured evidence bundle to a model after it steals credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets. Talos says the default model is Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, at a temperature of 0.2, and that if the model refuses, the malware tries Moonshot's Kimi K2 and then Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash. Talos says the prompt asks the model to act as a forensic intelligence analyst and to rank what the victim is worth. Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 1 that the call goes to OpenRouter and that the malware can skip the model step if no API key is supplied.

items.headline: Federal News Network: a CISA official calls Chainguard's early PHP patch release dangerous
items.summary: Federal News Network reported Oct. 30 that Jay Gazlay, CISA's acting associate director for vulnerability management, called Chainguard's decision to release PHP patches more than six hours before a coordinated disclosure dangerous and inappropriate. Gazlay spoke at an Oct. 28 conference hosted by Red Hat in Washington. Chainguard chief executive Dan Lorenc told Federal News Network he stands by the early release and said the company saw evidence the bugs were being exploited before the embargo. The PHP Foundation wrote that an attacker could study the fix while other PHP users were still waiting, and Federal News Network says CISA added the PHP bugs to the KEV catalog on Oct. 26.

items.headline: CISA adds Brotli and an Adobe Commerce bug to the KEV catalog, due Nov. 10
items.summary: CISA said Oct. 27 it added CVE-2026-48356, an Adobe Commerce and Magento unrestricted file-upload bug, and CVE-2026-111497, a Google Brotli unchecked-return-value bug, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The catalog sets a due date of Nov. 10 for both and describes the Brotli flaw as letting a remote unauthenticated attacker corrupt decoder memory, disclose memory, cause a denial of service, or potentially run code with a crafted compressed stream. SecurityWeek reported Oct. 28 that the Brotli bug, also called Node2Shell, affects Brotli 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, that federal civilian agencies were told to address it by Nov. 10, and that Broadcom warned Oct. 27 that SDDC Manager in VMware Cloud Foundation is affected because it uses Node.js, with patches still pending. SecurityWeek also said two honeypot operators logged attempts, and that ELLIO called the exploit it analyzed broken.

items.headline: Federal News Network: the CMMC task force lists a 90-day path to restart Phase 2
items.summary: Federal News Network reported Oct. 27, in the second part of its CMMC investigation, that a Defense Department task-force summary of the July request for information sorts reform options into changes the CIO could make without rulemaking, harder changes that may need rulemaking, and ideas outside the CIO's authority. The outlet says the summary, which it obtained, lists a 90-day option to restart Phase 2 for a narrower population, more guidance for assessors through the Cyber AB and CAICO, and an expansion of plan-of-action eligibility to 270 days that would require rulemaking. It also says the department wrote that clearer controlled-unclassified-information marking has the greatest potential to shrink the population that must implement NIST 800-171, and that the department declined to comment. Katie Arrington, who previously performed the CIO's duties, told Federal News Network the audit process has to start in order to be refined.

items.headline: Federal News Network: CMMC cost complaints in the RFI point at NIST 800-171, not the assessments
items.summary: Federal News Network reported Oct. 26 that the Defense Department reviewed 997 responses to its Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification request for information, 509 of them (51 percent) from the defense industrial base, and that an internal email lists NIST Special Publication 800-171 work, including Microsoft 365 GCC High, enclaves and inconsistent interpretation, as the top cost concern rather than CMMC itself. The outlet says the RFI put the average cost of CMMC, separate from NIST 800-171, at $47,000, and it quotes the department on that same average assessment cost, set against Kelly Loeffler's July statement that complying could cost as much as $600,000. Federal News Network says the review is past the 75 days Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies set in July, that the department declined to comment, and that as of September 2,433 companies had Level 2 third-party certifications.
